title: GOP Nominee Bo French Faces Backlash Over Post Targeting UT Students Who Look Indian
excerpt: The Republican nominee for Texas Railroad Commission drew condemnation from Senator John Cornyn, Governor Greg Abbott and Rep. Raja Krishnamoorthi after portraying diverse Longhorns fans as proof Americans are being 'displaced by foreigners.'
body:
• Bo French, the GOP nominee for the Texas Railroad Commission, posted photos on X of diverse University of Texas students celebrating the Longhorns' 24-23 comeback win over Ohio State on Sept. 12, calling the scene "a problem... far worse than anyone imagined."
  • A second post claimed social media was "exposing how many Americans have been displaced by foreigners" — drawing swift condemnation from within his own party.
  • Sen. John Cornyn called it "intolerance and racism"; Gov. Greg Abbott said "that is not my message"; House Speaker Dustin Burrows told French to delete the post.
  • The facts: Texas law requires at least 90% of UT Austin freshmen to be Texas residents; more than 80% of students are Texans and international students make up less than 10% of enrollment.

The posts

Bo French, the Republican nominee for the Texas Railroad Commission, ignited a firestorm on Sunday with a pair of posts on X targeting University of Texas students. Sharing a photo of a diverse group of students celebrating the Longhorns' 24-23 comeback win over Ohio State on September 12, French wrote: "I heard UT graduation this year looked like this. I didn't believe it. The problem is now obviously far worse than anyone imagined." An hour later he reposted the photo, adding: "Like body-cams exposed criminals, social media is exposing how many Americans have been displaced by foreigners. It's everywhere and far worse than any of us could imagine."

https://x.com/OccupyDemocrats/status/2099870286887739446

The students were football fans, not graduates — and there is no evidence any are foreign nationals. The backlash, including from his own party, was swift.

Republicans condemn one of their own

U.S. Senator John Cornyn of Texas led the response: "This is the Republican nominee for statewide office. Are other Republican elected officials going to condemn the intolerance and racism, or look the other way while it becomes normalized. This is how great political parties self-destruct. Sad."

"Are other Republican elected officials going to condemn the intolerance and racism, or look the other way while it becomes normalized? This is how great political parties self-destruct. Sad."

— Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas)

French fired back, accusing "RINOs like John Cornyn" of letting the state's institutions be "overrun by illegal aliens and foreign nationals." Texas House Speaker Dustin Burrows, also a Republican, said "you can oppose immigration policy without demeaning people because of their race and ethnicity" and called on French to delete the post. Governor Greg Abbott distanced himself: "That is not my message. A selective picture of Longhorn fans celebrating our biggest home victory ever actually shows a way that Texans unite" — even as Abbott pointed to his own support for strict immigration policies and freezing H-1B visas at universities.

Democrats piled on. State Rep. James Talarico, the Democratic Senate nominee, called it "blatant racism"; Ken Paxton — who beat Cornyn in the May 26 primary with Trump's backing — said he condemns racism "in all its forms." French's Democratic opponent, State Rep. Jon Rosenthal, a 25-year oil-and-gas engineer, said: "A man who can't tell a Longhorn from a foreigner has no business regulating anything in TX."

The facts behind the photo

The numbers collapse French's premise. Texas law requires at least 90% of UT Austin freshmen to be Texas residents; in 2025-26, Texans were more than 80% of students, with internationals under 10%. In 2024-25, enrollment was about 31.5% white, 25.5% Hispanic and 22.4% Asian — diverse and overwhelmingly American.

Vedant Nair, 24, a 2024 UT graduate, told Reuters his parents immigrated to Oklahoma from Mumbai in the 1990s; he was born in Oklahoma City and grew up in Dallas. "If you stripped away my name and skin color, I think my story is pretty similar to a lot of other Texans," he said. "All the other kids in that picture are just regular American kids." Sociologist Rodney Coates of Miami University said the remarks echoed longstanding anti-Asian narratives: "Hate is one of the easiest means of organizing."

Diaspora angle

The students French singled out were widely identified as South Asian Americans — and the condemnation from the community's own representatives was pointed. Rep. Raja Krishnamoorthi (D-Ill.) said French's "xenophobic hate toward South Asian students is disgraceful and part of a broader rise in attacks targeting South Asian Americans across the country."

"South Asian Americans are as American as anyone, and this kind of hatred has no place in our politics or our country."

— Rep. Raja Krishnamoorthi (D-Ill.)

What to watch

French is not retreating — on Monday he was fundraising off the controversy, writing "the radical left and their allies are attacking me" and asking supporters to donate. With early voting about a month away, SMU political analyst Matthew Wilson says the episode puts Texas Republicans in a bind: distance themselves from the comments without opening a feud inside the party. Whether voters punish the post at the ballot box is the next test.
image_caption: Bo French, Republican nominee for the Texas Railroad Commission. His posts about University of Texas students drew condemnation from Senator John Cornyn and other Republicans.
